MUQATIL:16:64-67/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r3.claim: Milk is purified between dung and blood, wholesome to drink, unlike either waste product.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r1.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r1.claim: Milk emerging between dung and blood is a sign that its Creator can also bring the dead back to life.

FARRA:v2p109/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p109/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p109/r1.claim: سائغا means the milk goes down without choking or sticking in the throat.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r1.claim: The pronoun in buṭūnihi refers to livestock as a collective; anʿām may be treated as masculine or feminine.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r2.claim: Milk is separated from the blood produced by digestion, while residue remains in the stomach; the drink is easy to swallow and does not choke.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245/r3.claim: Sāʾigh means easy to drink, without choking or catching in the throat.

TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r1.claim: Livestock provide a lesson: God gives people pure, pleasant milk from within their bellies, from between digested matter and blood.

TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r2.claim: Most Meccan and Iraqi readers, along with Abu Ja‘far, read نسقيكم with a damma on the initial nūn, as a continuing provision; most other Medinese readers and Asim use fatḥa.

TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r3.speaker: الكسائي
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r3.claim: Al-Kisa’i distinguishes أسقينا for providing a lasting drink from سقينا for giving one drink; Arabs can also vary the hamza in usage.

TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p269#2/r4.claim: Both readings are valid, but al-Tabari prefers the damma reading because it is common for continuous watering and livestock milk is continually available.

TAB-FULL:v14p271/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r1.speaker: بعض نحويي الكوفة
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r1.claim: A Kufan grammarian says the masculine pronoun refers to النعم, a collective equivalent to الأنعام; Arabic poetry uses masculine agreement with a collective meaning.

TAB-FULL:v14p271/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r2.speaker: بعض نحويي الكوفيين
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r2.claim: Another explanation is “what is in the bellies of what We mentioned,” using masculine agreement for a generic thing or person; poetry and 6:78, 80:12, and 27:35 illustrate the construction.

TAB-FULL:v14p271/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r3.speaker: بعض البصريين
TAB-FULL:v14p271/r3.claim: A Basran grammarian says the phrase means the bellies of whichever livestock have milk, with “milk” understood; al-Tabari judges the first two explanations better Arabic.

ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r3.claim: Sibawayh and al-Khalil distinguish giving someone a drink from providing water, though both forms may mean the same.

ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r4.claim: An unattributed verse uses سقى and أسقى; the author says its wording can support either account.

ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r5.claim: Anʿām is a collective noun that may be masculine or feminine; another verse says what is in their bellies.

ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r6.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p208/r6.claim: Milk emerging between dung and blood demonstrates a power that only God can exercise.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r10.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو جعفر وأبو عمرو والكوفيون إلا عاصما
NAHHAS:v2p400/r10.claim: They read ‘We give you drink’ with a damma on the initial nūn.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r11.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r11.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
NAHHAS:v2p400/r11.claim: They distinguish saqā as handing someone a drink from asqā as providing a watering place or supply.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r12.speaker: أبو عبيدة
NAHHAS:v2p400/r12.claim: He treats the two verbs as dialectal synonyms.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r13.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p400/r13.claim: He explains saqā as offering a drink and asqā as praying for rain or providing water; Abu Ubayda also allows asqā to mean saqā.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r14.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
NAHHAS:v2p400/r14.claim: He judges the open-nūn reading better suited to the verse’s sense.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r15.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v2p400/r15.claim: The best explanation of the masculine singular ‘its bellies’ is that Arabs use a singular predicate with livestock, whose collective noun can be masculine or feminine.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r16.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r16.speaker: الكسائي
NAHHAS:v2p400/r16.claim: As relayed by al-Farra, the phrase means the bellies of the livestock already mentioned.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r17.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r17.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v2p400/r17.claim: Anʿām and naʿam are both collective plurals, allowing masculine agreement; Arab usage and an anonymous verse attest this usage.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r18.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r18.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
NAHHAS:v2p400/r18.claim: The poem’s word naʿam witnesses the collective noun’s use with masculine agreement.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r19.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r19.speaker: أبو عبيدة
NAHHAS:v2p400/r19.claim: The phrase means the bellies of whichever animals produce milk, since not all livestock do.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r20.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r20.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p400/r20.claim: The phrase ‘pleasant for drinkers’ is an adjective describing the milk.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r8.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p400/r8.claim: The livestock and its milk are a sign of God’s power and sound governance.

NAHHAS:v2p400/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p400/r9.speaker: عاصم وشيبة ونافع
NAHHAS:v2p400/r9.claim: They read the verb ‘We give you drink’ with an open initial nūn.

SULAMI:v1p368#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p368#2/r1.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v1p368#2/r1.claim: Livestock are subdued and obey their owners, while humans rebel against their Lord and disobey Him.

SULAMI:v1p368#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p368#2/r2.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ
SULAMI:v1p368#2/r2.claim: God made livestock carry people and their burdens despite being unaccountable; an innocent creature thus carries a sinner.

THALABI:v6p26/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
THALABI:v6p26/r1.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash say أنعام is masculine or feminine: feminine by collective sense, masculine by its form and lack of a same-form singular.

THALABI:v6p26/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r2.speaker: الكسائي
THALABI:v6p26/r2.claim: Al-Kisa'i says the pronoun refers to the intended sense of what is in the animals' bellies.

THALABI:v6p26/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p26/r3.claim: Other grammarians explain the masculine pronoun as deictic reference to this thing or person, supported by several poetic examples.

THALABI:v6p26/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r4.speaker: المؤرج
THALABI:v6p26/r4.claim: Al-Mu'arrij says the pronoun refers to the relevant part of the herd, since only milk-bearing animals provide milk; the word milk is implicit.

THALABI:v6p26/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p26/r5.claim: Farth is the contents of the stomach; milk is pure because it is separated from dung and blood, and it is palatable and does not choke drinkers.

THALABI:v6p26/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p26/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the animal's food separating in the stomach: blood flows into veins, milk into the udder, and dung remains.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r1.claim: God's making people drink what is in livestock's bellies expresses that He permits them to drink it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r2.claim: خالص means pure, free of dung and blood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r3.speaker: ابن بحر
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r3.claim: Alternatively, خالص means white; al-Nabigha's use of خالصة الأردان refers to white sleeves, with green shoulders referring to sword straps.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r4.claim: سائغا may mean lawful for drinkers.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r5.claim: Alternatively, سائغا means that the drink does not repel the drinker; milk does not cause choking.

QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r12.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r12.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r12.claim: Milk emerging pure between dung and blood displays divine power; the One who preserves it can preserve gnosis amid the many forms of spiritual lapse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r1.claim: The commentary refers to its explanation of ʿibra under the verse about lessons for people of insight.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r2.claim: With an open initial nūn, nusqīkum means We give you drink until you are satisfied; scripture uses this form for drinking by the mouth.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r3.claim: He prefers the reading with a damma, as it conveys continuous, plentiful drinking; asqā commonly expresses providing a lasting drink.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r4.claim: He explains the masculine pronoun in their bellies by treating anʿām as a collective-gender noun that can be masculine or feminine; another verse uses the feminine.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r5.speaker: سيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r5.claim: He likewise treats anʿām, though shaped as a plural, as a masculine singular collective such as qawm or nafar.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r6.claim: He says naʿam and anʿām are equivalent, so the masculine pronoun follows the masculine meaning naʿam; he supports such sense-based agreement with poetry.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r7.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r7.claim: The cited rajaz line uses masculine agreement with naʿam, supporting the masculine form.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r8.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p107#4/r8.claim: He reads the pronoun as referring to what was mentioned, supplying an understood word such as animals.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r1.claim: He cites a line about chicks with masculine agreement for their entrails, a parallel for masculine agreement with the collective livestock noun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r2.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r2.claim: Arabic can use masculine agreement for an understood generic thing: the sun is called this when it rises, and a gift sent by a woman is followed by the masculine verb when Solomon receives it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r3.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r3.claim: The line he recites about Afraʾ treats the feminine name with masculine agreement, illustrating generic masculine reference.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r4.speaker: الأحمر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r4.claim: His line about Umm ʿAmmar supplies another example of masculine agreement with a feminine referent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r5.claim: The examples use an implied masculine generic such as thing or person; true feminine nouns still require feminine agreement in standard speech.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r6.speaker: المؤرج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r6.claim: He proposes that the pronoun points to omitted milk: the phrase means from the milk in their bellies, since not all livestock produce milk.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r7.speaker: صاحب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p110/r7.claim: He prefers and elaborates the implied-milk analysis: the general term includes animals without milk, so the phrase singles out the milk-bearing subset and omits milk because it is understood.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r1.claim: Farth is the dung or chyme of the stomach; Ibn Abbas identifies it as feed inside the stomach.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r2.claim: In a report through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih, food settles in the stomach with dung below, blood above, and milk between; blood enters veins, milk the udder, and dung remains.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r3.claim: Pure milk has no admixture of blood or dung; sāʾigh means that it passes easily and pleasantly through the throat.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r4.claim: The transformation of one kind of fodder into several products inside an animal demonstrates the Creator's power and oneness to a reflective person.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r5.speaker: أصحابنا
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p113/r5.claim: They infer that human semen is not impure merely because it is inside the body beside impurities, as milk emerges pure beside blood and dung; semen can remain pure even through a path of impurity.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r1.claim: Livestock provide a sign of God's power and oneness: pure milk is produced between digestive waste and blood and is easy to swallow.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r10.claim: Farth is the solid residue that descends into the animal's stomach; sāʾigh is what passes easily through the throat.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وحفص عن عاصم وحمزة والكسائي
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r4.claim: They read نسقيكم with a ḍamma on nūn, from asqaynāhu.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r5.speaker: شيبة ونافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم ويعقوب
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r5.claim: They read نسقيكم with fatḥa on nūn, from saqaynāhu; Abū ʿUbayd prefers it because this is continuous drinking.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r6.speaker: قيل
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r6.claim: Another explanation treats the two forms as dialectal synonyms.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r7.speaker: الكسائي
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r7.claim: He distinguishes the forms: asqā provides an ongoing drink, while saqā gives one drink; Labīd uses both, and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā considers al-Kisāʾī's distinction stronger.

JISHUMI:v6p4062/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r9.speaker: الخليل
JISHUMI:v6p4062/r9.claim: He defines ʿibra as learning from what has passed; the word can mean a sign or proof, as in the call to people of insight.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r10.speaker: الكسائي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r10.claim: He refers the pronoun to mā, meaning the things mentioned earlier.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r11.speaker: المؤرج
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r11.claim: He refers the pronoun to a part or portion, with milk understood as an omitted noun.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r6.claim: Livestock offer a lesson: pure milk comes from between digested matter and blood and is easy for drinkers to swallow.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r7.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر ويعقوب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r7.claim: These readers open the initial nūn in nusqīkum; the other readers use ḍamma, and both are dialect forms.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r8.speaker: الفراء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r8.claim: He refers the pronoun in butūnihi to naʿam, equivalent to anʿām.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة والأخفش
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p27/r9.claim: They say naʿam can be masculine or feminine: feminine for its collective sense, masculine according to its form.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r1.claim: Farth is the heavy material in a stomach and is no longer called that after it exits; milk is free of blood's color and excrement's smell.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r2.claim: Sāʾigh means pleasant and passing easily through the throat; it is also said that no one has ever choked on milk.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28/r3.claim: He says fodder settles and is ground in the stomach: excrement below, milk in the middle, blood above; God directs blood to veins, milk to the udder, and leaves excrement in place.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r1.claim: Sibawayh treats al-anʿām as an indeclinable-looking plural in the form of a singular; this explains its masculine singular pronoun, unlike the feminine plural in 23:21.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r10.claim: The first min is partitive, since milk is part of the livestock's contents; the second marks the starting point between dung and blood, or modifies milk as an earlier circumstantial phrase.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r11.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r11.claim: Some who hold semen pure argue that its passage through the urinary tract does not make it impure, just as pure milk emerges between dung and blood.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r2.claim: Al-anʿām may be a broken plural of naʿam or a singular collective with plural meaning; it can take a masculine singular pronoun or feminine agreement according to the intended sense.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r3.claim: A poetic line uses naʿam with masculine singular agreement to illustrate the collective noun's grammatical behavior.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r4.claim: Nasqīkum is read with either fatḥa or ḍamma as a fresh statement answering how the lesson is seen.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r5.claim: God creates milk between dung and blood, with a barrier of divine power preventing either from affecting its color, taste, or smell.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r6.claim: One account describes the animal's digestion as dung below, milk in the middle, and blood above; the liver sends each substance to its proper destination.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r7.speaker: شقيق
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r7.claim: Shuqayq defines sincerity as separating action from flaws, just as milk is separated from dung and blood.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r8.claim: Sāʾigh means easy to pass through the throat; he says no one has ever choked on milk.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p574#2/r9.claim: The word is read sayghan with a doubled or light consonant, on the pattern of hayyin and layyin.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r8.claim: Anʿām comprises camels, cattle, sheep, and goats; ʿibra is the state from which one draws a lesson.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p404/r9.claim: Readers differ on whether نسقيكم begins with a fatḥa from saqā or a ḍamma from asqā; some lexicographers call the verbs synonymous, while others distinguish single versus repeated watering.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r1.claim: Abu Raja reads يسقيكم with a yāʾ, meaning God gives you drink; another group reads تسقيكم with a feminine tāʾ, a weak reading also discussed in Sura al-Muʾminun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r2.claim: The pronoun in مما في بطونه can refer to the animal kind as a collective or to anʿām understood as the singular naʿam.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r3.claim: Another explanation takes the pronoun as referring to some animals, since males do not produce milk.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r4.claim: Farth is material that descends into the intestines; sāʾigh means easy and pleasant to drink.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r5.claim: One group reads siyghan with a doubled yāʾ, while ʿIsa al-Thaqafi reads it with a silent yāʾ as a lightened form; the root is wāw-based, from sawagha.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405/r6.claim: A report says milk has never choked anyone, and another attributes this statement to the Prophet.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r1.claim: Livestock—camels, cattle, and sheep—are an instructive sign of God’s power and wondrous design.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:16:66-67/r2.claim: Al-Kalbī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that fodder settles in the stomach: the lower part becomes dung, the upper blood, and the middle milk; blood enters the veins, milk the udder, and dung remains unmixed.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r3.claim: The milk is pure, without blood or dung, and pleasant to swallow; the liver distributes these substances according to divine design.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r4.claim: For those who deny resurrection, the one who can extract drinkable white milk from dung and blood can likewise bring the dead from earth without mixing their bodies with others.

TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r1.claim: The continuation of the agreement discussion allows the pronoun to refer to the milk-bearing animals intended, and min may be partitive because only some livestock produce milk.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70/r1.claim: For ‘We give you drink,’ Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Yaʿqūb, and Sahl read with fatḥa on nūn; the rest use ḍamma, while Abū Jaʿfar reads with tāʾ in al-Muʾminūn.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r10.speaker: الصلتان العبدي
TABRISI:16:66-70/r10.claim: Al-Ṣaltān al-ʿAbdī’s line shows agreement based on meaning: two feminine nouns are treated as a masculine dual subject.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70/r2.claim: The two verbs may distinguish handing someone a drink (saqaytu) from providing water (asqaytu), or asking God to water someone; others treat them as synonyms or distinguish a single drink from ongoing provision.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r3.speaker: ذو الرمة
TABRISI:16:66-70/r3.claim: Dhū al-Rumma’s line uses asqaytu for providing or asking that someone be watered, with the speaker sharing his grief with stones and dwellings.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABRISI:16:66-70/r4.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says saqaytu is for giving a drink once, while asqaytu can describe giving drink continually.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r5.speaker: لبيد
TABRISI:16:66-70/r5.claim: Labīd’s line uses both verb forms for the tribes, supporting their synonymous use.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70/r6.claim: The ‘lesson’ is an instructive sign; farth is material that descends into the stomach, and sāʾigh describes food that passes easily through the throat.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r9.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:16:66-70/r9.claim: The pronoun in ‘its bellies’ can agree with al-anʿām as a masculine collective; another explanation refers it to one animal, as in a poet’s wording that returns to milk.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r1.claim: These readers pronounce nusqīkum with a ḍamma, also at the parallel verse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r10.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r10.claim: Sāʾigh means easy to drink without choking; another says it is pleasant despite emerging between dung and blood.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r11.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas describes fodder separating in the stomach into dregs, blood, and milk; the liver directs blood to veins and milk to the udder.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r2.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r2.claim: These readers pronounce nusqīkum with a fatḥa in both locations.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r3.claim: Abu Ja'far reads tisqīkum with an open tāʾ at both locations.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r4.claim: The work previously explained cattle, the meaning of “lesson,” and the distinction between saqā and asqā.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r5.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r5.claim: Al-Farra says anʿām and niʿam are equivalent plurals, so the masculine pronoun refers to the semantic masculine niʿam; a poem likewise shifts to the singular meaning milk.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r6.speaker: الكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r6.claim: Al-Kisa'i says the pronoun points back to what was mentioned in the bellies, with a poem as evidence.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r7.speaker: المبرد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r7.claim: Al-Mubarrad calls this a common Quranic pattern, where a demonstrative or verb refers to an understood thing rather than the feminine noun itself.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r8.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r8.claim: Abu Ubayda says the pronoun refers to some of the cattle, since only some cattle produce milk.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r9.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p462#3/r9.claim: Ibn Qutayba says anʿām may be masculine or feminine; farth is stomach contents, from which milk is purified after blood and dregs separate.

RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r4.claim: The verse turns from celestial evidence to the wonders of animals; ʿibra was explained earlier as an instructive sign for those with insight in Q 3:13.

RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r5.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وحفص عن عاصم وحمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r5.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hafs from Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read نسقيكم with a damma on the initial nūn; the remaining readers use a fatha.

RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p51#2/r6.claim: The fatha means giving drink, while the damma means furnishing a drink; here the latter suggests abundant, continuing supply, and Abu Ubayd prefers it because drinking is continuous.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r1.claim: The singular masculine pronoun in بطونه can refer to al-anʿām, a collective singular by form but plural feminine by sense, hence the different form in Q 23:21.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r2.speaker: الكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r2.claim: Al-Kisa'i parses بطونه as the bellies of what was mentioned; al-Mubarrad says such usage is common in the Quran, as in Q 6:78 and Q 74:54-55.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r3.claim: This masculine reference works only for grammatically nonreal feminine nouns; it cannot be used for a genuinely female person or maidservant.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r4.claim: A third grammatical explanation supplies an omitted اللبن: you are given to drink what is in its bellies, namely milk, since not all cattle yield milk.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r5.claim: Farṯ means the dung or contents of the rumen.

RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v20p52/r6.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says fodder settles in the rumen: the lower part becomes dung, the upper blood, and the middle milk; blood enters the veins and milk the udder, while dung remains, so the milk is pure.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r1.claim: The cause that produces milk from blood in females is absent in males, explaining the difference.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r2.speaker: المفسرون
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r2.claim: Commentators say dung, blood, and milk form in one place: dung at the bottom of the rumen, blood at the top, and milk in the middle.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r3.claim: Razi rejects that account as contrary to observation and experience; if blood formed in the stomach, it would have to be vomited, which is clearly false.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53#2/r4.claim: He explains the phrase as a sequence: milk comes from some parts of blood, which comes from subtle parts of the food in the rumen; God filters coarse matter and gives the remainder properties suited to milk and a child's body.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r1.claim: Razi rejects the claim that blood and milk form in the rumen: repeated slaughter shows neither there, and a process observable in some cases would have been seen.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r2.claim: His account is that food is digested first in the stomach or rumen; subtle material is absorbed into the liver and dense residue passes to the intestines.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r3.claim: The liver's second digestion turns subtle nourishment into blood and separates bile, black bile, and water; blood then travels through veins and undergoes a third digestion before the udder transforms it into milk.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r4.claim: Males are hot and dry while females are cold and moist; females need added moisture both to form the fetus and to let the body stretch as it grows.

RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p53/r5.claim: After birth, moisture that nourished the fetus is redirected to the breast or udder to nourish the infant.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r1.claim: The stomach's lower outlet closes while food is needed for digestion and absorption, then opens to release residue; this timed control bespeaks a wise agent.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r2.claim: The liver selectively draws subtle parts while the intestines draw dense residue; reversing those powers would disrupt the body's interests.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r3.claim: The liver cooks subtle material into blood, while the gallbladder, spleen, and kidney draw off bile, black bile, and excess water, leaving nourishing blood; this specific allocation requires an all-knowing planner.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r4.claim: Blood nourishes the fetus in the womb, then is redirected to the breast for milk after birth and to the whole body once the child grows; the changing route tracks need and wisdom.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r5.claim: Tiny nipple pores act as a filter, allowing fine milk through while retaining coarse material, so the milk is pure and suitable for the child.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r6.claim: God inspires the infant to suck, allowing it to benefit from the milk created in the breast.

RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p54/r7.claim: Milk contains fat that is hot and moist, water that is cold and moist, and curd that is cold and dry, qualities not present in grass; successive transformations show a wise, merciful creator manages the world for human interests.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r1.claim: Sāʾigh means flowing easily and pleasantly through the throat; the wording is linked to Q 14:17.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r2.speaker: أهل التحقيق
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r2.claim: The creation of milk also demonstrates the possibility of resurrection: water and earth become plants, plants become blood, blood becomes milk, and milk yields fat and cheese, showing God can restore dead bodies to life and reason.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r1.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r1.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says cattle and naʿam are the same, and naʿam is masculine, so the pronoun returns to that masculine lexical equivalent.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r2.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī explains masculine agreement by the collective genus sense and feminine agreement in 23:21 by the group sense.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r3.speaker: القاضي إسماعيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r3.claim: Qāḍī Ismāʿīl infers from the masculine pronoun that a wet nurse’s husband contributes to milk kinship; the report says the woman provides milk and the man conception, and the issue is treated in 4:23.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r4.claim: Milk emerging pure between excrement and blood displays God’s power; food is processed in the stomach, milk separates from blood in veins, and excrement remains behind.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r5.claim: Farth is dung that descends into the stomach; when it exits, it is no longer called farth.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes fodder settling in the stomach, separating into lower excrement, middle milk, and upper blood, which the liver distributes to veins and udder.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r7.speaker: ابن بحر
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#2/r7.claim: Milk is pure from blood redness and excrement filth despite sharing one vessel; Ibn Baḥr instead glosses pure as white, supported by al-Nābigha’s verse.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r1.speaker: النقاش
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r1.claim: Al-Naqqāsh and others use the verse to argue that semen is pure, comparing it to milk emerging through the urinary tract; Ibn al-ʿArabī rejects the analogy as ignorance because milk is described as a blessing and sign.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r2.claim: Al-Qurṭubī counters that semen is also a great favor because it produces honored human beings, citing 86:7 and 16:72; if impurity comes from passage through urine, it is acquired while the substance remains pure in origin.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r3.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r3.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and others hold semen pure; ʿĀʾisha scraped dried semen from the Prophet’s garment, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ also scraped it.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares semen to mucus and says to remove it with a reed or wipe it with a cloth.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r5.claim: The report that ʿĀʾisha washed semen may reflect removing something distasteful rather than legally impure, reconciling it with reports of scraping.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r6.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r6.claim: Mālik, his school, al-Awzāʿī, and Kufans consider semen impure; reports differ from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿĀʾisha, while Mālik calls washing it from wet-dream clothing obligatory by their consensus.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r7.claim: Milk from a dead animal cannot be used because a pure liquid is held in an impure udder; human milk after death is disputed according to whether a person becomes impure at death.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#3/r8.claim: Either view on a dead woman’s milk still permits milk kinship, since a child can be nourished by it; the prophetic definition covers milk that grows flesh and strengthens bone.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r1.claim: Sāʾighan means pleasant and easy to swallow; lexical forms describe drink passing smoothly, and al-Kumayt’s sawāghan is something that relieves choking.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r2.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r2.claim: A report says no one has ever choked on milk, and this is also attributed to the Prophet.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r3.claim: The verse permits enjoying sweetness and delicious food without opposing asceticism, provided it is lawful and not excessive.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r4.speaker: أنس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r4.claim: In an authentic report, Anas says he served the Prophet drinks from his cup including honey, nabīdh, milk, and water.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r5.claim: Some reciters disliked falūdhaj and milk with a meal, but most scholars permit them.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r6.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r6.claim: When Mālik ibn Dīnār refused falūdhaj at a table, al-Ḥasan urged him to eat it, noting that cold water involved more extravagance.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r7.claim: Abū Dāwūd and others transmit from Ibn ʿAbbās a prophetic supplication after food for blessing and better provision, and after milk for blessing and more milk because nothing else suffices for both food and drink.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r8.claim: Scholars explain milk’s special status as the first nourishment, which grows bodies, sustains them, and is free of the harms of other foods.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#4/r9.claim: The commentary says God made milk a sign for Gabriel in guiding this community, then introduces the authentic report.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#5/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66#5/r1.claim: The preceding discussion concludes that milk is blessed and that asking for an increase points to fertility, goodness, and abundant blessing.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r1.claim: The cattle here comprise camels, cows, sheep, and goats; they are a lesson demonstrating God's power, unity, and greatness.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r2.claim: ʿIbra originally compares one thing with another to grasp its reality, as in 59:2; Abū Bakr al-Warrāq says the cattle's submission to people contrasts with people's rebellion against their Lord, and an innocent bearer carrying a sinner is a great lesson.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r3.claim: The first reading nusqīkum, with an open nūn, is used by Medinans, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr; others including Ḥafṣ use the damma form usqīkum.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r4.claim: The two readings may be dialectal variants; another account distinguishes giving water directly from providing a watering place or cause to drink, attributed to Ibn ʿAzīz and supported by Labīd's verse.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r5.claim: A weak variant reads tasqīkum with tāʾ, referring to the livestock, while another reads yasqīkum with yāʾ and makes God the subject; the two main forms are associated with Quraysh and Ḥimyar.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r6.speaker: سيبويه
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r6.claim: For the masculine pronoun in min buṭūnihi, Sībawayh says Arabs can give a singular predicate to the feminine plural cattle noun; Ibn al-ʿArabī objects that this appeal does not suit Sībawayh's rank or discernment.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r7.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r7.claim: Al-Zajjāj says cattle, as a collective genus, may be masculine or feminine, allowing the masculine pronoun.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r8.speaker: الكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:66/r8.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says the pronoun refers to what was mentioned; he cites the masculine pronoun in 80:11–12, and also allows the sense some of the animals since males have no milk, a view followed by Abū ʿUbayda.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r10.claim: The first مِن is partitive, while the second marks origin or the location from which drawing begins; خالص means pure of blood color, dung odor, or coarse matter, and سائغ means easy to swallow.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r11.claim: The milk description is also read سيغا, with doubled or light consonant.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r4.claim: Livestock offer an instructive sign that carries one from ignorance to knowledge; the pronoun is masculine here for the collective's grammatical form, unlike the feminine in al-Muminun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r5.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر ويعقوب
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r5.claim: These readers pronounce نسقيكم with an a-vowel here and in al-Muminun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r6.claim: Milk derives from selected fine portions of blood formed from digested food; Ibn Abbas's account of rumen layers, if sound, means precursors rather than completed milk and blood.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that ingested fodder becomes excrement below, milk in the middle, and blood above in the animal's rumen.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r8.claim: The actual process involves the liver separating waste and humors, directing surplus fluids, then routing excess after pregnancy and birth to the udders to become milk.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:64-66/r9.claim: Reflection on the creation of humors and milk, their pathways, causes, and governing powers compels recognition of divine wisdom and mercy.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r1.speaker: نافع والشامي وأبو بكر
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r1.claim: These readers vocalize the initial nūn with fatḥa in the verb 'We give you drink.'

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r2.speaker: الزجاج
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r2.claim: Al-Zajjāj says saqaytu and asqaytu have the same meaning.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r3.claim: Anʿām is a singular-form noun on the pattern afʿāl, so its pronoun is singular; in 23:21 the feminine plural reflects its collective meaning.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r4.claim: God creates pure milk between dung and blood, separated by a barrier so neither gives it color, taste, or smell; the organ distributes the digested feed into blood, milk, and residue.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r5.claim: An account says feed is cooked in the animal's stomach: residue settles below, milk in the middle, blood above; the liver directs each to veins, udders, or stomach, where the residue descends.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r6.claim: This process is evidence for reflection; Shuqayq defines sincerity as separating work from defects as milk is separated from dung and blood.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p261#4/r7.claim: The milk is easy to swallow, and it is said no one has ever choked on milk; the first min is partitive, while the second marks the starting point.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r1.claim: After rain revives earth, the text recalls the life of familiar livestock sustained by rain-grown plants and highlights milk emerging between dung and blood as a great sign.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r2.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, along with al-Ḥasan, Zayd b. ʿAlī, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr, Nāfiʿ, and Medinans, reads نَسْقِيكُم with fatḥa on nūn (from سقى); the other seven readers use ḍamma (from أسقى).

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r3.speaker: أبو رجاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r3.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads يُسْقِيكُم with passive-like ḍamma on yāʾ; its subject may be God or, according to the cited authority, the livestock as a benefaction that supplies drink.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p553/r4.claim: A group including Abū Jaʿfar reads تُسْقِيكُم with feminine tāʾ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it weak, but the author says feminine agreement with the livestock and masculine agreement with its collective gender are both sound.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r1.speaker: الكسائي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r1.claim: For the masculine singular pronoun in بطونه, al-Kisāʾī supplies the understood phrase 'the bellies of what We mentioned'; others explain the singular by treating the non-rational broken plural as a collective or referring to a subset of milk-bearing livestock.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says الأنعام is a singular noun on the أفعال pattern and explains the singular pronoun; feminine بطونها elsewhere reflects its collective sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p554/r3.claim: The author corrects al-Zamakhsharī's account of Sībawayh: Sībawayh distinguishes plural patterns that can resemble singulars, and says أفعال may exceptionally refer to one, not that الأنعام is conventionally singular.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r1.claim: Sībawayh explicitly says أفعال is not a regular singular noun pattern; al-Zamakhsharī therefore distorted his wording and misunderstood the point that the pattern can exceptionally take singular agreement.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r2.claim: نسقيكم مما في بطونه explains the sign: it says how the lesson occurs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats the clause as a fresh explanation: God creates milk in the middle between enclosing dung and blood, with a divinely established barrier keeping their color, taste, and smell from affecting it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes fodder settling in the stomach: its lower part becomes dung, upper part blood flowing in veins, and middle part milk flowing to the udder.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r5.speaker: ابن جبير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p555/r5.claim: Ibn Jubayr places dung in the middle intestines, blood above, and milk between them; the liver directs them respectively to stomach, veins, and udders.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r1.claim: Al-Rāzī says the commentators' account of all three substances forming together in the stomach contradicts observation and experience: slaughtered animals have no visible blood or milk there; digestion sends dense matter to intestines and clear matter to liver, where it becomes blood and is separated into components.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r2.claim: In al-Rāzī's physiological account, purified blood travels from liver through veins to the soft udder and changes into milk.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r3.claim: Al-Rāzī also explains the verse causally: milk derives from some blood, and the blood derives from subtle parts of digested food originally in the dung, so milk comes from what lay between dung first and blood second.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r4.claim: The wording allows 'between' to be spatial, as commentators say, or figurative for the causal progression al-Rāzī describes; he records both possibilities despite al-Rāzī's objection to the spatial sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r5.claim: The two من phrases can modify نسقيكم while bearing different meanings, partitive and origin; alternatives take من بين as a circumstantial phrase or as an appositive to ما.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p556/r6.claim: Some read سيغا with doubled yāʾ; ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar reads a light form like هين from هين. سائغ means easy to swallow and pleasant.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r1.speaker: حديث
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r1.claim: A hadith says that no one has ever choked on milk.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.claim: The opening and closing of the livestock sign frame the passage: reason is needed to recognize its lesson.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.claim: God says We give milk because animals supply it without human processing; for fruit drinks people process produce, so the verse says you make them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.claim: Milk is presented before fruit drinks and honey because people need it more and it is natural nourishment; the Prophet chose milk when offered milk, wine, and honey on the Night Journey, and the sequence matches the rivers of Paradise.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r1.claim: In مما في بطونه, من can mark partitive meaning or origin.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r10.claim: The poem فيها خطوط uses feminine reference to the described thing.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r11.claim: Non-rational broken plurals allow collective or plural agreement: this verse takes plural sense, while al-Muminun takes collective sense; poetry illustrates plural treatment.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r12.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r12.claim: The pronoun may stand for an understood singular with collective meaning, like نعم; the supporting analogies continue in the next segment.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the masculine singular pronoun refers to الأنعام as a singular-pattern word on أفعال; the Shaikh disputes the citation of Sibawayh.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r3.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r3.claim: The Shaikh explains Sibawayh's point: plural patterns that can be further pluralized resemble singulars, unlike the terminal مفاعل and مفاعيل patterns.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r4.claim: Sibawayh says أفعال may sometimes stand for one thing, as in هو الأنعام, figuratively meaning نعم.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r5.claim: The Shaikh argues قد يقع للواحد indicates occasional figurative use, not an inherent singular pattern; Sibawayh elsewhere excludes أفعال from singular nouns.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r6.claim: The author finds al-Zamakhshari's reading sufficient to license singular agreement and says he has not misquoted Sibawayh.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r7.claim: The pronoun may refer to female livestock only, because males do not produce milk.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r8.claim: Al-Kisa'i glosses it as “in the bellies of what was mentioned.”

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#2/r9.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Quranic demonstratives can refer to “the thing,” citing 80:11 and 6:78; feminine agreement is grammatical, not natural.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#3/r1.claim: The poem تركنا الخيل والنعم uses نعم collectively, supporting the implied singular explanation.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r1.claim: من بين فرث may attach to the drinking verb as origin; if the preceding من has the same governor and sense, it must instead be بدل. A partitive first من avoids that problem.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r2.claim: It can be a circumstantial phrase modifying لبنا; al-Zamakhshari says it is fronted because it is the lesson's central point.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r3.claim: A third analysis makes من بين فرث a circumstantial phrase for the preceding relative pronoun.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r4.claim: فرث is fodder residue in a stomach or thick remaining food in the intestine; related verbs mean crushing a liver or bringing calamity.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r5.claim: لبنا is the second object of نسقي; سيغا is read with doubled ياء or, by Isa ibn Umar, lightened; it cannot be a verb, which would have to be سوغا.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r6.claim: A related view supplies a collective singular such as لبن for plural ألبان; an anonymous verse illustrates it.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r7.speaker: سيبويه
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r7.claim: The analogy أحسن الفتيان وأجمله means “the best young man,” but is not productive among Sibawayh and his followers.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r8.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r8.claim: Abu al-Baqa offers the bull as antecedent because milk is attributed to the male; the author rejects it as unnecessary and inconsistent with multiple bellies.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r9.speaker: مكي
SAMIN-DURR:16:66#4/r9.claim: Maki transmits the bull interpretation from Ismail al-Qadi without objection.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r1.claim: نسقيكم can explain the lesson by answering an implied “how is it a lesson?”

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r10.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r10.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls feminine تسقيكم weak; the Shaikh guesses agreement with feminine الأنعام, but the author says gender can vary by aspect.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r11.claim: The author instead finds it semantically weak: the blessing is attributed appropriately to God, not the livestock.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r2.claim: Alternatively, it predicates an omitted هي العبرة, answering the same question.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r3.claim: Nafi, Ibn Amir, and Abu Bakr read نسقيكم with fatḥa on نون here and in 23:21; others use damma.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r4.claim: One view says سقى and أسقى are synonyms; a poem uses both for wishes of rain and abundance.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r5.speaker: أبو عبيد
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r5.claim: Abu Ubayd distinguishes watering lips (سقى) from watering crops and land (أسقى); rain prayers use أسقى.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r6.speaker: الأزهري
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r6.claim: Al-Azhari says water from livestock, sky, or a river is أسقيت; for the lips, Arabs say سقى.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r7.claim: Al-Farisi distinguishes giving someone enough to drink (سقيته حتى روي) from supplying a river as drinking source (أسقيته نهرا).

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r8.claim: Another view uses سقاه for handing over a cup, not أسقاه.

SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:66/r9.claim: Abu Raja reads يسقيكم; its subject may be God or a pronoun for the livestock.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.claim: Camels, cattle, and sheep are signs of the Creator's power, wisdom, gentleness, and mercy.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r2.claim: The singular pronoun in 'from its belly' can refer to the collective livestock as a singular or to the animal itself; the plural appears in 23:21, while singular reference to money appears in 74:54–55 and 27:35–36.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r3.claim: As food is digested, blood passes to the veins, milk to the udder, urine to the bladder, and dung to the outlet; each remains separate and uncontaminated.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r4.claim: The bodily products do not mix after separating, which leaves the milk pure and easy to drink.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r1.claim: Livestock milk is a sign because it is purified from dung, blood, and other admixtures and remains easy to drink.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r2.claim: Most readers pronounce nusqīkum with ḍamma, from asqā (providing drink); Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim in Shuʿba’s transmission pronounce it with fatḥa, from saqā (giving a drink).

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r3.claim: Anʿām is a collective noun treated as masculine singular; the masculine pronoun in “its bellies” is unambiguous because the milk comes from females.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains that fodder in the animal’s rumen separates into dung below, milk in the middle, and blood above; the liver distributes them to their respective places.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r5.claim: Farṯ is the heavy material that descends to the rumen and ceases to be called farṯ once it leaves; sāʾigh means easy passage through the throat.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r1.claim: Livestock comprises camels, cattle, sheep, and goats; their milk is a sign carrying people from ignorance to knowledge.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj says asqā and saqā both mean to give someone drink; another lexicon says asqā grants ongoing watering while saqā gives a single drink.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r3.speaker: الكسائي
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r3.claim: The pronoun in ‘their bellies’ refers either to female livestock, since only they give milk, or to the whole class previously mentioned.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r4.claim: The preposition ‘from’ marks milk’s origin between the rumen’s residue and blood; the rumen is the animal’s counterpart to a human stomach.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r5.claim: Pure milk has neither blood’s color nor offal’s smell, and passes easily down the throat; it is said that nobody chokes on it.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r6.claim: A prophetic report recommends asking blessing over food and milk and says the speaker knows no food or drink more beneficial than milk.

BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r7.speaker: الكواشي
BURSEVI:v5p36#2/r7.claim: Al-Kawashi describes the stomach separating fodder into residue, milk, and blood; divine power keeps them unmixed, while the liver routes blood to veins, milk to udders, and residue onward.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r1.speaker: سيبويه
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r1.claim: Sibawayh elsewhere says أفعال is not a singular pattern, prompting grammarians to reconcile his remark that الأنعام can be singular.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan reconciles the statements by taking singular الأنعام as a figurative use for the collective النعم, not a singular by form or lexical convention.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r3.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r3.claim: Al-Khafaji sees no contradiction: the two pattern groups differ because some may form further plurals; he says some Arabs genuinely used أتى and الأنعام as singulars, though rarely.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r4.claim: Under the rare singular usage, the pronoun refers to الأنعام by form; if it is plural, it may refer to an implied portion, its female animals, or the collective sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r5.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176#2/r5.claim: Al-Bahr explains the masculine singular pronoun by grammatical gender of the collective, even when it occupies the place of a plural noun, citing a comparable Arabic phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r1.claim: An ʿibra is something by which one crosses from ignorance to knowledge; its root sense is crossing from one place to another, and here it is magnified as a great lesson.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r2.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r2.claim: Al-Raghib says ʿubūr specifically refers to crossing water by swimming or the like, though common usage is broader.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r3.claim: The clause نُسقيكم is an explanatory response to an implicit question asking how the livestock provide a lesson; an extra implied subject is unnecessary.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r4.claim: The singular masculine pronoun in بطونه is explained by treating الأنعام as a collective noun and referring to its grammatical form, though it can also be feminine or plural by meaning.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r5.speaker: سيبويه
ALUSI-FULL:v14p176/r5.claim: Sibawayh's discussion appears inconsistent: he says some Arabs use أفعال for a singular and cites الأنعام, but elsewhere says that pattern is only plural.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r1.speaker: الكسائي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r1.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says the pronoun is singular masculine by assuming a singular antecedent, just as a singular demonstrative may follow a group noun; al-Alusi notes that this works only with grammatically feminine groups.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r10.claim: Razi's account says blood travels to the udder, where God transforms it into milk.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r2.claim: The objection that الأنعام is broader than نعم is answered by saying that those who call it a plural either use نعم broadly or distinguish them by usage and kinds.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود والحسن وزيد بن علي وابن عامر ونافع وأبو بكر وأهل المدينة
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r3.claim: These readers pronounce نسقيكم with an open nūn, treating it as the verb saqā, which some dialects use like asqā; a line by Labid witnesses that usage.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r4.speaker: بعض
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r4.claim: One lexical distinction is that saqā means giving someone a drink, while asqā means providing water to livestock or land; another says the former means quenching and the latter preparing drink.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r5.speaker: أبو رحاء
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r5.claim: Abu Rajaʾ reads يسقيكم with yāʾ and a damma, referring to God; al-Lawamiʿ also permits reference to the livestock, which al-Alusi regards as strained.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r6.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads تسقيكم with feminine tāʾ; Ibn Atiyya calls this weak, but al-Alusi says gender variation is not a flaw because the forms reflect different aspects of the collective.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r7.speaker: الصحاح والبحر
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r7.claim: The lexicons define فرث as dung while it remains in the stomach, or as the dense remainder of food in the stomach or intestine.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says that after fodder is digested in the rumen, its lower part is excrement, middle part milk, and upper part blood, taking بين literally.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r9.speaker: الرازي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p177/r9.claim: Al-Razi rejects milk and blood forming in the rumen because slaughtered animals show neither there; he explains digestion through the stomach, liver, vessels, and udder, where blood is transformed into milk.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r1.speaker: النبي عن يحيى بن عبد الرحمن ابن أبي لبيبة
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r1.claim: A Prophetic report says no one drinks milk and chokes, since God calls it pure and easy to drink; the author gives no grading.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r2.speaker: فرقة وعيسى بن عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r2.claim: One group reads سيغا with a doubled yāʾ; ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar reads سيغا with a light yāʾ, like the shortened form of هين.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r3.claim: The verse supports the purity and permissibility of milk from edible livestock; some also analogize that semen can be pure despite passing through the urinary channel.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r4.speaker: أهل التحقيق
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178#2/r4.claim: People of verification argue that milk's transformation from grass and water into milk, butter, and cheese demonstrates the Creator's power to restore dead bodies to life and intelligence.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r1.speaker: الرازي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r1.claim: On the physiological explanation, milk arises from parts of the digested food and then blood, so between is figurative; an explanation of Ibn Abbas's report makes the middle part milk material and the top blood that nourishes the body.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r2.claim: A trusted observer told al-Alusi that blood can emerge from the udder after milk when milking is prolonged, supporting the account he recounts.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r3.claim: The first من is partitive and the second marks the starting point between blood and excrement; both attach to نسقيكم with distinct senses, and لبنا is its second object.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r4.claim: Fronting the prepositional phrases before لبنا creates anticipation, especially because the sources described contrast sharply with the pure milk; alternatively من بين لبنا can be a fronted circumstantial phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r5.claim: Another parse treats both من as origin markers and من بين as an appositive of inclusion to the preceding phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p178/r6.claim: خالص means either purified of dense matter by the narrow passage or free of the color and smell of blood and excrement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r1.claim: This is another proof and blessing arising from livestock; the sign is integrated into the benefits of animals in Q 16:5–7.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r2.claim: Milk sustains human life as rain sustains the earth, and rainfall helps form milk through the pasture it produces.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r3.claim: The phrase about pure milk between waste and blood displays God's craftsmanship and wisdom, while the verse also emphasizes the gift to people.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r4.claim: The verse continues the sign in Q 16:65: just as attentive listeners learn from rain, they can learn from livestock; the address shifts from third to second person and is doubly emphatic.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r5.claim: الأنعام is a collective noun for camels, cattle, sheep, and goats; عبرة means a lesson to heed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r6.claim: The clause “We give you drink from what is in their bellies” explains what the lesson in livestock consists of.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r7.claim: The belly means the whole digestive cavity; من in مما is source-oriented because milk is secreted from fodder, though it may be partitive if it refers to milk while passing through the digestive system.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p199#2/r8.claim: The من before “between dung and blood” is extra, emphasizing the milk's intermediate position.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r1.claim: Saying “We give you drink” rather than “you drink” combines the blessing with the sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r2.claim: Fodder is digested through the stomach and liver and becomes liquid in the udder, secreted as dung and blood are also produced.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r3.claim: فَرْث is digestive residue moving into the intestines; blood is processed by the liver and circulated through the heart and vessels, as discussed at Q 5:3.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r4.claim: Milk is produced while waste and blood are secreted; blood passing through vessels near the udder is processed by mammary glands, like kidneys and intestines separately producing their outputs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r5.claim: بين is not literal space between layers; it figuratively marks a middle rank, like courage between recklessness and cowardice, making the description accessible at different levels of knowledge while remaining accurate.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r6.claim: Milk is intermediate: it is not blood, which remains in vessels, and not foul waste, because it is pure, nourishing, and useful.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p200/r7.claim: The phrase “between dung and blood” describes the milk and is fronted as a circumstantial phrase because it is the focus of the sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
