IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r1.claim: Since milk is made in the udder, it is the direct object of نسقيكم; “from what is in their bellies” specifies its source, not its location, and its order makes that syntax clear.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r2.claim: Pure means free of impurities from urine and feces; palatable means it passes easily and safely, without the harmful properties of blood.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r3.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this concise account of milk formation a scientific sign, beyond what Arabs of the time could know and difficult for a naturalist to describe more briefly.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r4.claim: The singular pronoun in بطونه follows الأنعام as a grammatically singular collective noun; Arabic can instead follow its plural meaning, as in Q 23:21.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r5.claim: خالص means pure and unclouded; سائغ means easy to pass through the throat.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p201/r6.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb read نسقيكم with fatḥa on the nūn; Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf use ḍamma; Abū Jaʿfar reads it with ت, referring to the livestock.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.claim: This adds one blessing to another; both concern drink and pressing by hand, and Arabs could call pressing grape juice “milking,” as Ḥassān's poem witnesses.

TABATABAI:16:65-67/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r4.claim: Farth is material entering the stomach and intestines, becoming manure only after discharge; sāʾigh describes food or drink that passes smoothly down the throat.

TABATABAI:16:65-67/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r5.claim: The livestock lesson is pure, untainted milk drawn from the proximity of dung in the stomach and blood in vessels around the udder; this marvel demonstrates power to resurrect people after their bodies decay.

ASAD-NOTES:16:66#n75/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:16:66#n75/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:16:66#n75/r1.claim: Milk is a glandular secretion neither needed by the mother's life nor eliminated as useless to metabolism, explaining its description as between waste and blood.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r1.speaker: İbn Atıyye; Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r1.claim: The term an‘am for milking livestock is said to cover sheep, goats, cattle, and camels.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r2.claim: God nourishes the earth with rain and grows animal feed; milk formed from that feed is a human food, singled out for its nutritional value and as a sign of wise creation in both its benefit and bodily formation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r3.claim: Fers refers to food residues whose nutrients have been absorbed and that will become waste; milk is between this useless residue and blood needed by the animal, and benefits drinkers after secretion.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r4.speaker: Zemahşerî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r4.claim: Another explanation is that milk passes between the systems of waste and blood without mixing with either; divine power separates it so its color, taste, and smell remain pure.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:66/r5.claim: The author also suggests that nutrients partly enter blood and partly leave as waste, while milk is another product made from nutrients that nourishes others and tastes pleasant.

QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#1/r1.claim: Form I nasqī gives drink directly, removing the causative layer of Form IV nusqī.

QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:16:66:8#2/r1.claim: The feminine third-person makes the livestock the grammatical subject and agent of giving drink.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r1.claim: Cattle provide warmth, food, transport for burdens, and beauty; this verse adds milk as a blessing for which people should be grateful.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r2.claim: Milk is also one of the four rivers of the Garden.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r3.speaker: Ibn Hishām
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r3.claim: Ibn Hishām's account says the Prophet chose milk over wine on his Night Journey and was told he had been guided to fiṭrah, primordial purity.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r4.claim: Milk's primordial purity is symbolically contrasted with wine's associations of maturity and age.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r5.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r5.claim: Nusqīkum can mean that cattle provide a perpetual source of drink, with replenished milk through most of their lives.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r6.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r6.claim: Milk is not contaminated by the refuse and blood present in the animal and issuing from it.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r7.speaker: Z
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r7.claim: Commentators say a barrier among the fluids prevents blood or refuse from affecting milk's color, taste, or smell, so it remains pure.

STUDYQURAN:16:66/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r8.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
STUDYQURAN:16:66/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah likens pure milk to Sufism's middle path between merely external Sharīʿah and pursuing truth while ignoring external requirements; he also compares spiritual training between sober wayfaring and ecstatic attraction to a barzakh between two seas.
